audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding fixed-strict penultimate (stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 01010 (1 = a stressed syllable)) rests on George 2009:507 / 1993:430, the specialist reconstructive statement for an extinct language, and every source opened agrees on penultimate primary stress: StressTyp2 dump (George 1993:430, Pool 1958:6, Smith 1955:6) confirmed verbatim in the held SQL dump; held Toorians Middle Cornish grammar sec.1(c); held Jenner 1904 p.54; and four Cornish Language Partnership documents downloaded now (Bock et al. 2010 p.5; Bock 'basics' p.1). Nothing suggests the classification is wrong; the Williams/George 'prosodic shift' dispute concerns quantity/rhythm and pitch, not stress position. Two weaknesses keep it short of well-sourced: (1) the record's quote/cite/grade fields are empty and the deciding George text is not yet obtained (read at silo.pub, unsaved), so the verbatim p.507 check cannot be done in custody; (2) the secondary-stress clause (4th/6th from end)

sources.citation: George, Ken. "Cornish", in Ball & Müller (eds.), The Celtic Languages, 2nd edition, Routledge 2009, chapter 11 (pp. 488-535); Stress section read verbatim at pp. 506-507. Accessed via full text embedded at silo.pub (https://silo.pub/download/the-celtic-languages-second-edition-routledge-language-fa…
sources.quote: "Normal stress in polysyllables: The primary stress fell on the penultimate syllable, and a secondary stress fell on the fourth and sixth syllables from the end. This applied to most polysyllables, including close compounds." (p. 507, running head CORNISH 507). Also p. 506: "There is very little textual evidence as to how Cornish was stressed. Evidence from placenames suggests that the pattern was the same as in Breton ... Unpublished work by Keith Bailey on stress in Middle Cornish verse sugges

sources.citation: Bock, Albert; Bruch, Benjamin; Kennedy, Neil; Prohaska, Daniel; Rule, Laurence. 2010. Pronunciation and Variants: A Supplement to An English-Cornish Glossary in the Standard Written Form. MAGA / Cornish Language Partnership (version 14/08/2010).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: "Stress normally falls on the last syllable but one (the 'penultima'). In loose compounds, primary stress falls on the second component, e.g. penn BLOODH. ... In close compounds, it falls regularly on the penultimate syllable. Following a convention established since the time of R. M. Nance, irregular or unpredictable stress has been marked in the glossary by inserting a dot after the stressed vowel."

sources.citation: Bock, Albert. n.d. (c.2008-2010). 'What the fuss is all about.. some basics of the Cornish reconstruction debate' [, kernewegva.com], 10 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: "Only two out of the three accentual features are clear: the second-last syllable in a word was normally the loudest (i.e. it was stressed) and, at the very least until the time of the Ordinalia, it was also the longest one. We have no idea if it also carried the highest pitch." Also frames the Williams 'Prosodic Shift' vs George debate as being about rhythm/length, not stress position.

sources.quote: Stressed syllables are louder and longer (long vowel or long consonant/cluster); no independent placement rule beyond examples with penultimate stress (TERMyn, PASSys, TRIGys, SeLEVen).
